doc.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997

title: Menza's band history and wanting to work with Basie
summary: Menza lists his employers, regrets not playing with Basie, and praises Buddy Rich as the only real bandleader.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: And you both have been with Louie Bellson on and off — Don for quite a while, right?

My stints were Stan Kenton — I mean in the beginning it was Al Boletto with a band out of New Orleans, and then Maynard Ferguson, Stan Kenton, and then the European thing with the Max Greger Big Band in Munich; and then coming back I went with Buddy Rich and then Louie Bellson and of course Henry Mancini, I worked with Henry for like almost 30 years. But I have to say in all the band leaders that I worked for, Buddy was the one. It’s a great shame I didn’t get to work with Basie. I talked with Basie a couple of times. He heard me play with Louie and he said, “I’d like you to play with the band sometime,” and my heart started beating. I would have loved to have gone on that band and played with that band. And it’s after the fact now. I don’t want to do it with the ghost band, I wouldn’t consider it. But to have done it when Basie was there, and been around him, and been able to like have hands on with all the history, yeah, that would have been a thrill. Because my likes lean towards that kind of big band, and that kind of swing, that kind of energy. I loved it. But getting back to it evolving, because like this has to be documented, Buddy Rich was the only real band leader I ever worked for. He told you the truth, mediocrity did not exist in his vocabulary. He was very hard on people and he expected them to give as much as he did in the band. But if something went wrong with the band, I mean if something happened, if there was any kind of scene, he pushed © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

everybody out of the way and he’d say, “You deal with me, this is my band.” And some of the leaders, and they were all very good, they’d back up and, “It’s your problem, you deal with it, you got it.” Buddy was incredible. He knew exactly what he wanted out of a piece of music, and he’d sit out front, he didn’t read — he had a lot of insecurities and he never gave you that impression by how he played. He had a lot of insecurities. He didn’t read any music. He didn’t know a lot about music, except he knew what was good and he knew what he liked. Nothing more, nothing less. And if you stood up to play and you stepped on it, you can be sure you’d never stand up and play again.
